facts.text: I wrote an application example and asked Damian to remember all details about me and Drongo's writing style.
My research focuses on nano functional neural interfaces (nFNIs).
My penultimate goal is to design and safely implement a system for high-resolution, bidirectional communication with the nervous system that is minimally invasive.
I have been interested in creating this system since I was in elementary school.
I took part in the 2020 summer undergraduate research program in Computational Neuroscience hosted by Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh.
Due to the coronavirus, the 2020 summer undergraduate research program internship was converted to an online format.
During the 2020 program, I worked in Dr. Aaron Batista’s lab under the guidance of his graduate student Erinn Grigsby.
In the 2020 program, I studied “Decoder Performance Classified as a Function of Neurons.”
In the study, we investigated the impact of neuron dropping on decoder performance.
I used Matlab to create three different Kalman filters and linear regression decoders.
Each decoder contained different position, velocity, and velocity-position decoders to test robustness to neuron dropping.
Despite coronavirus challenges, we virtually presented our work at the Center of the Neural Basis of Cognition.
I am continuing my research into brain-computer interface decoders with my partner.
My current decoder research investigates how modulation depth and preferred direction factor into decoder performance as neurons are dropped.
My senior thesis at Worcester Polytechnic Institute involves a team under the guidance of Dr. Dirk Albrecht investigating dosing of deep brain stimulation (DBS).
My senior thesis team investigates DBS in disorders including Parkinson’s Disease, dystonia, essential tremor, and epilepsy.
My senior thesis team aims to optimize the procedure for finding the correct DBS dosage of frequency, pulse width, and voltage for each unique individual.
My senior thesis team uses C. elegans as a model system because of the animal’s completed connectome.
I am conducting a formal independent study into neural nanotransducers.
In my independent study, I hypothesize that nFNIs can be used as a relay system to send and receive external devices’ signals.
In my independent study, I propose that an imaging nFNI would receive information of a neuron firing and transduce the signal.
In my independent study, I propose that a nearby relay nFNI would relay the signal until it reached the skull where the signal could be read.
In my independent study, I propose that the process functions conversely for signals sent to a specific neuron.
My current theory is that nanowires composed of magnetic nanoparticles bound together by a protein chain could act as relay nFNIs.
My current theory is that magnetoelectric nFNIs at the end of the nanowires would send and receive signals.
My current theory is that the wire would self-assemble using proteins and insulate the signal to reduce noise.
My current theory is that the wire would attach itself to the skull and the targeted neuron for direct stimulation.
I want to make this concept into my dissertation at Rice University.
I plan to continue my work at Rice University to design and implement a minimally-invasive, bidirectional brain-computer interface using nFNIs.
After my time at Rice University, I hope to found a research company centered on further research into nFNIs and making this BCI safely usable by humans.
Ultimately, I hope the BCI would be a versatile treatment option for neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s Disease by allowing direct activation and monitoring of affected neurons.
I hope the BCI could enhance neuroprosthetics by allowing sensations such as touch to be sent back to the brain.
I hope to continue this work at Rice University because I will get guidance I could not receive anywhere else.
I have been doing the creation of this system as my life’s work since I was in middle school.
